About this work

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's reply to eight questions the Emperor set before him: on faith and understanding, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles worked by unbelievers, on witches and malefic magic, and on related theological points. Composed in 1508 and among the most widely read of his shorter treatises, it became his central statement on witchcraft and was drawn on heavily by later demonological writers. The eight questions are set out in an enumerated table at the head of the book, and Trithemius answers each in turn with his characteristic mixture of scholastic authority and pastoral caution.

This is the 1534 Cologne edition (Bavarian State Library scan), one of two print witnesses of the Octo Quaestionum in this corpus (the other is the 1601 Mainz edition, prdl-70286). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No complete English translation of the work has been published — only excerpts have circulated — so this is offered as the first open, freely reusable rendering of the full text. [unclear] 8 Cal. 1950 [unclear] 15th century 1482 [unclear] THE BOOK OF EIGHT QUESTIONS OF JOHANNES TRITTENHEMIUS, ABBOT of Sponheim, which Emperor Maximilian proposed to him for resolution.

  1. On faith and understanding. 2. On the faith necessary for salvation. 3. On the miracles of unbelievers. 4. On sacred Scripture. 5. On the reprobate and evildoers. 6. On the power of sorceresses. 7. On divine permission. 8. On the providence of God.

A little work exceedingly useful and pleasant, now printed for the first time.

TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST UNCONQUERED lord of the world, Emperor Maximilian: the preface of Johannes Trittenhemius, Abbot of Peapolis, to the book of eight questions.

I have obeyed your commands, most unconquered Emperor Maximilian, and the eight questions which you proposed to me some time ago, when I had been summoned to your Highness at the castle of Boppard, I have resolved with what brevity I could and set down in this form of a little book. You wished, moreover, if I remember rightly, that, so far as could be done, I should follow the way of nature in their solution, for the sake of those who grant less to belief. Yet this did not seem possible to me in all cases, because the subject matter of the questions in most places rested on theological rather than natural principles. For even if the Christian religion, among the sects of all mortals, is held to be nearer to the laws of nature, more conformable to them, and closer to them, nevertheless the principal articles of our faith are not all provable according to the common way of nature.

This, we must necessarily believe, was done so that faith too might have its place, and firm belief not lack its own merit. And so, having entered as far as my strength allowed upon a middle path of disputation at your command, I have used the testimony partly of nature and partly also of the divine Scriptures. For truly, the things which it befits us to believe are not to be rashly examined by human arguments, since, as holy Gregory says, faith has no merit where human reason supplies the proof. Therefore, with fear of God and reverence for our undefiled Christian religion, I have determined to answer the proposed questions in such a way that I depart from the definitions of the Roman Church neither in jest nor in earnest. Hence whatever I have ever written, or shall write, I wish to be wholly subject to its determination and judgment.

On faith and understanding

Question First

The first question of your most serene Majesty was this: Why did almighty God wish rather to be believed by mortals than to be known and understood, namely in that mode of knowledge and understanding by which he is known and understood by the holy angels?

I remember that I answered this question, put before me in person by your most sacred Majesty, as follows: Almighty God, who is intellect without beginning, pure, everlasting, and unchangeable, existing above every position knowable to us, far more perfect than infinite perfections, by his most wise will created from nothing, at the beginning, two intellects, namely the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, at the beginning of its creation, was made in act with respect to all knowable things, and knew all things; but the human intellect at first consists in potency to all things, yet is ignorant of all things. At the end, however, through many and continuous upward movements, it will become like the angelic intellect, knowing both God and all things that pertain to the cognition of the promised knowledge and understanding. The angelic and human intellects differ as any two opposites do: as act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, possession and privation, beginning and end, the immovable and the movable, substance and accident, truth and likeness, nature and art, health and sickness, whole and part. For the angelic intellect is like act, light, knowledge, possession, beginning, the immovable, the immediate, simple substance, truth, nature, and the whole. But the human intellect is like potency, darkness, ignorance, privation, end, the movable, the mediated, the composite, accident, likeness, art, and part. Hence whatever belongs to the angelic intellect from the beginning, these same things are present in the human intellect at the end, after it has laid aside the burden of the flesh. For just as beginning and nature perfect the angelic intellect, so the end and art, after many exercises at last, raise the human intellect upward. Therefore between these two intellects there is great inequality at the beginning, though at the end they are finally made equal, when the human intellect will be as great by art as the angelic intellect was before it by nature. Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect, as soon as it was created, knew all things from the beginning, without any action or motion of its own, by immovable substantiality and by nature.

Question One

that it could understand, and that, created in an instant, it came forth full and perfect in all knowledge. But the human intellect, since it was created in all ignorance and privation, and was destined for the body for its own exercise and by degrees, must by continual action, motion, and art come to the knowledge of God and of all things. The end will at last make it equal to the angelic intellect, changing its potency into act and bringing it forth from mere potency and possibility into essence; from empty it will make it full, from imperfect perfect, from deprived possessed, from dark luminous, from nocturnal diurnal, from lunar solar, and from earthly heavenly. This cannot happen while the mind is bound in the body, as the Christ-loving Saint Paul says: As long as we are in the flesh, we are away from the Lord.

To know God belongs to a pure, simple, and perfect intellect; but the human intellect, so long as it dwells in the body, is impure, mixed, unstable, and imperfect, and for this reason, without faith, wholly ignorant of the knowledge of God and of heavenly things. The object of each intellect, both human and angelic, is the same: that highest and immutable good, God, the one principle of all things, to which they return by a natural desire for knowledge. But the angelic intellect, if compared with the human, is as nature is to art, and as simple intellect is to reason, which touches the principles of learning; but reason, through the principles, proceeds to conclusions. Hence it is manifest that the angelic intellect immovably apprehends its proper object, to which the human intellect, through the angelic medium, after many exercises of its own, as has been said, at last, by reasoning, prepares an ascent for itself. The human intellect, however, is separated, by the medium of angelic knowledge, from the perfection of its natural object, and therefore is necessarily mobile, returning through that medium to its own principle. For every motion proceeds from an extreme through a medium to an extreme; but where there is no medium, the extremes are already immediate and near, and for this reason immovable.

But the human intellect, placed as it were in a dark prison, as long as it is held in the body, is moved by sense and reason toward understanding, though confusedly and all too imperfectly, and therefore it has a medium between itself and God, which we have called angelic. Wisdom 9. The body appointed to it is a very great impediment to perfection, as a certain lover of wisdom said: The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the sense that thinks many things. Therefore it was wholly necessary for us to believe God rather than to know or understand him, because it is utterly impossible for that superdivine and uncircumscribable majesty to be comprehended by us, who understand nothing without the ministry of the senses and the discourse of reason. But God, existing far above every position, remains subject neither to mortal senses nor to reason, just as he is read to have said to Moses: Man shall not see me and live. Hence also the divine evangelist John says: No one has ever seen God. Nor is it any wonder. For since God is the first and eternal intellect, most pure, most simple, most perfect, immovable, incomprehensible creator, highest, and far above every position immense and uncircumscribable, he could not be comprehended by the human intellect, which is impure, subject to composition, imperfect, mobile, created, comprehensible, lowest, and constituted under the measure of position.

As for the question that seemed to arise from the first, whether God, since he is almighty, could have made himself knowable to the human intellect in the same way as to the angelic, I say that no one of sound mind has ever denied that God can do all things. Those things that imply a contradiction, we say God cannot do, because they are contrary to the order of wisdom, immutable as it disposes all things, just as the destruction of construction of the whole is not doubted to be contrary at the same time; and if I shall say For it was neither fitting, nor could it in any way have come to pass, that God should be comprehended by the human intellect. For if mortal man, by the guidance of human nature, comprehended the immortal God, then certainly he would have to be called no longer man, nor mortal, but an angel; and either man would become comparable to God, or God to man. For so long as the angelic intellect stands between, the human intellect cannot understand God. But it stands between until the death of the flesh, when the mind, having obtained its natural freedom, will become wholly equal to an angel.

You now see, I believe, most manifestly, Emperor, that it was neither fitting nor possible that the human intellect should comprehend the divine, the created the creator, the temporal the eternal, the changeable the unchangeable, the weak the omnipotent, since, as a certain philosopher says, there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. And therefore it is necessary for mortals to believe in the immortal God, whom we cannot comprehend by any manifest reasoning.

Although the order of the whole universe providently declares the author of all things, and although we understand that nothing apart from him was produced without a beginning, nevertheless what God is and in what manner he is the human mind cannot grasp, since he is far above all things that we can understand concerning him, or anything mortal whatsoever, and is far outside and above every affirmation, as holy Dionysius says. Indeed, he is neither soul nor sense, nor imagination or opinion, nor reason, nor intelligence; nor does he have reason or intelligence.

Nor is he spoken of, nor understood. He is neither number nor multitude, nor order, nor magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality; neither likeness nor unlikeness. He neither stands nor is moved; neither does he produce rest, nor does he have power, nor is he power. He is neither light, nor does he live, nor is he life. He is neither substance, nor age, nor time; nor is there spiritual contact of him. He is neither form, nor truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom; neither one nor unity, nor deity or goodness; nor is he spirit, so far as we can know. Nor is there for him the denomination of son or father, nor anything else among those things that are known to us or to anyone else in the world. Nor is he anything of those things that are not, nor of those things that are; nor do the things that are know him as he is. There is no speech of him, nor name, nor knowledge. He is neither darkness nor light, neither error nor truth; nor is there of him any affirmation at all, nor negation. For he is above every affirmation, the perfect and singular cause of all things. And his excellence is above every negation, namely the excellence of him who is simply absolved from all things and is above all things.

Therefore we say, as Dionysius says, that since as the cause of all things he is above all things, he is neither without substance nor without life, nor does he lack reason or mind. Nor is he a body, nor figure, nor species, nor does he have quality or quantity or mass; nor is he in a place, nor is he seen. Nor does he have sensible touch, nor does he sense, nor is he sensible. Nor is he subject to rashness or disturbance, agitated by fleshly passions; nor is he weakened by being subject to sensible accidents. Nor does he need light; nor does he admit change or corruption or division or increase; nor is he, or does he have, anything else belonging to sensible things.

Hence, since he is far above every affirmation and excels it, he could not be comprehended by a creature placed beneath him, which necessarily uses the senses for understanding, as the Peripatetic truly said: “There is nothing in our intellect unless it has first been in sense.” Therefore God, who is not subject to the senses of mortals, far exceeds the human intellect. According to affirmative affirmation, he truly is altogether in all things; and according to negative removal, by which one approaches more closely, he is none of all the things that are subject to the cognition of mortals. Indeed, since he is above all things, he cannot be any of those things that are subject to him. For this reason Empedocles beautifully gave the similitude, saying: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere. Let the human intellect now raise itself as much as it can.

Let the human intellect now raise itself as much as it can; and if it strives to comprehend God, let it rightly understand and comprehend the center of this imagined sphere, together with its circumference ending nowhere. But if it is not sufficient to understand this proposition of its own likeness, why does it contend to investigate the essence of God, which exists above every positive assertion?

May it not weary you, most unconquered Caesar, to hear another likeness concerning God from Cusanus, once a cardinal priest of the Roman Church, my fellow Mosellan, a man most learned in those times. He says: God is a straight line of infinite length, which makes a circle. Let us see, then. If the line is straight, how does it make a circle? But if it makes a circle, how is it straight? For a circle and a straight line are naturally opposed. Nevertheless, a line of infinite length, since it has neither beginning nor end, necessarily makes a circle, although it is proposed to be imagined not as curved but as straight.

Since, therefore, God is infinite, greatest without quantity, best without quality, all things in all things without circumscription, above all things without excluding positive assertions, it was not possible for him to be comprehended by the circumscribable human intellect, which uses the service of the senses for understanding; and what is promised to it, when at last purified, in the fatherland could not be granted to it, confused and impure, on the way. But after our mind, at last released from the flesh, has come to its own center, which is God, clean, simple, pure, perfect, and consummated, then, made equal to the angels, we shall know God perfectly and all things, just as Saint Paul says to the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 13: We see now through a mirror and in an enigma; but then face to face.

For this reason we said that the angelic intellect, by the guidance of its nature, cleaves immovably to its own principle, because it is pure act and habit; and since it is simple by natural condition, it cannot be impeded by any commerce with composition. But the human intellect, as has now been sufficiently declared, since it is potency and privation, is impure because of its commerce with its body, and is indeed delayed from perfect act until at last, released from the flesh, it passes into the fellowship of likeness with the angels; then for the first time it is to be admitted to the true knowledge of God. But if in the meantime the affection of love necessary for salvation is joined to present Christian faith and to future divine knowledge, the same everlasting blessedness prepared with the holy angels will be given to the worshippers of God. But if, however, the depraved mind, through too much commerce with its flesh, has despised the love of God, ## Question Two

then the intellect, released from its prison, will indeed go forth, exalted in knowledge to the measure naturally belonging to it; but it is so much the more wretched, the more it is found through evil will to be like the demons. Therefore, to conclude the solution of the proposed question as far as I have been able, I say that it is not possible for almighty God to be understood perfectly by us as long as we, being mortal, dwell in the flesh.

On the faith necessary for salvation.

Question Second

The second question of your unconquered Majesty was this: Since today only a small part of the world is subject to the laws of the Christian faith, whether that opinion of very many people seems admissible without injury to truth, who think that each person, in his own religion, which he believes to be true and salutary, as a worshipper of the one God, outside the Christian faith and without baptism, can be saved, provided that nothing is known concerning the religion of Christ. To answer this question simply, according to your intention, I have judged more than enough for the common understanding, since I know that today there are many among Christians who [unclear] impiety for the salvation of man of lost men, makes God out to be cruel. But because a cause of just consideration moved Your Most Serene Highness to ask these things, not because you do not know what must be held in this matter according to the Catholic faith, but so that you might have something true to set against those who attack the truth, I shall answer the questions briefly, as best I can.

If anyone could be saved outside the Christian faith, Christ, the Son of almighty God, would seem to have become man superfluously and without cause. For if there is salvation outside Christ, then Christ is not the Savior of all. But because it was necessary that the only-begotten Son of God, for the salvation of the human race, be born as man in the world, suffer, die, and rise again on the third day according to the Scriptures, he did not come into this world in vain, nor superfluously, nor without cause. Since this is so, whoever asserts that anyone can be saved outside the faith of Christ shows himself not a Christian, but an adversary of the faith and a deserter of Christ. For whoever does not believe in Christ, the Son of God, promises himself eternal salvation in vain. For he who is the truth, Jesus Christ, says in the holy Gospel: He who does not believe will be condemned. And again: He who does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And again, a little later, he adds, saying: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. The holy Apostle also says: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Hebrews 11.

The solution of the proposed question is now clear to all who truly believe in Christ: salvation is through him, the Savior of the world, and whoever does not believe in him cannot be saved. Nor is it lawful for a Christian in any way to go beyond the boundaries of his religion, so as to presume to explain this question otherwise than Christ has taught. Whoever goes outside this rule of faith by asserting the contrary is plainly shown not to think rightly about Christ, the Savior of the faithful. For whoever promises salvation to anyone outside Christ wishes to declare Christ a liar. But we, confirmed by the most sacred ordinances of the Gospel, firmly believe and without doubt pronounce that no one can be saved outside the faith of Christ, however much he worships one God, however holy or just his life, however much he trusts in his paternal religion or in another. Christ is salvation, and outside the Christian faith no one will be saved. For why would Christ the Son of God have willed to die for the sins of the world, if each person could have been saved outside his faith in his own paternal tradition? From the beginning of the world, after the fall of the human race, it was impossible for anyone to be saved unto eternal life otherwise than in the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. What of the fact that the greater part of humanity today remains outside the faith of Jesus? Did not the Savior of the world himself long ago foretell in the holy Gospel: Many are called, but few are chosen? And again he says: Enter through the narrow gate, because wide is the gate and spacious is the way that leads to perdition, and there are many who enter through it.

What do we think our salvation can contribute to God, who has no need of good things? For whether many are saved or many are damned, God himself is the unchangeable Lord of all. Nothing is added to him if all are saved; nothing is lacking to him if the whole world perishes. The order of the providence of the divine majesty is infallible; it embraces those who are to be damned no less than those who are to be saved, each and every one. Certainly no one among those to be damned suffers injustice, since, just as in the first man we all fell, so no one is saved except in the blood of Jesus Christ through mercy, and no one is damned except in his own unbelief and according to desert through justice. From the foregoing another question arises.

From what has been set forth there arises another question of no small difficulty, which human curiosity is accustomed to raise against those who think rightly about the faith of Christ: Why does almighty God, since he is just and merciful, not cease creating so many thousands of human beings whom he has most certainly foreknown are to be damned? Why does he not spare the wretched, and why would he bring forth to destruction, in such great multitude, those whom he foreknew would turn aside to evil? For it would seem better not to exist than to exist badly.

Let him answer this question, if anyone thinks himself God’s counselor. Who am I, that I should explain the cause of the divine will? For the Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, and there is no one who can resist his will. Hence a certain wise man says to God: “Who will hold it against you, if the nations you made perish?” The Almighty established for things an order of succession, which he will never revoke by any regretful change. For just as he permits his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, so until the end of the age he allows human beings, pious and impious, to be conceived, born, and grow.

The thoughts of human beings are not in God, nor does he change his counsel because of time; but since he is unchangeable and everlasting, willing all things together and once for all, he has from eternity preordained all things invariably. Once does God speak, as Sacred Scripture bears witness, and he does not add to it, because whatever he wills he wills immovably and admits no change. Therefore God permits, by a most just reason, that human beings should be born good and evil, pious and impious, faithful and faithless, sinners and saints, those to be saved and those to be damned: he who assigned this order to all things. Nothing perishes to God, who is Lord of all; and Christ Jesus, no less over evil than over good human beings and spirits, everywhere holds his empire strengthened: God from God the Father without time, and man from the Virgin in time, appointed mediator of God and human beings. He is the one through whom we have access to God; he is the savior of all the faithful. A man thinks wrongly of him if he rashly concedes that anyone can be saved without the Christian faith.

The omnipotence of God has regard to the order of things that he established, according to whose inviolable sequence of rectitude no one will be saved without faith in Christ; no one who does not believe in the Son of God is justified. Therefore they are moved by a vain and utterly foolish piety who think that anyone outside the faith of Christ, in the whole world and in any sect whatever, is to be saved, since his judgment is manifestly to the contrary. Let them hear the Savior himself again saying in the Gospel: “No one comes comes to the Father except through me; for I am the way, the truth, and the life.” If no one comes to the Father except through the Son, surely no one will be saved except through him. Who will save the Jew or the pagan, when no one can be saved except through Christ?

But Christ will undoubtedly save only those who believe in him in heart, speech, and deed. He will not save the Jew, not the Saracen, not the pagan, not any other unbeliever, because they do not believe in him, but despise his teaching; they contemn the same man, and, blaspheming his holy name, scorn him all day long. For he himself said in the Gospel: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him I too will be ashamed before my Father and his holy angels.”

Tell me now, you who worship Christ and contend that someone can be saved outside the Christian faith in his own sect, which he thinks true: do you believe the Gospel of Christ to be true or false? If true, why do you hold the contrary to it? For Christ says: “Whoever has not believed in the Son of God, the wrath of God remains upon him.” And also: “He has already been judged.” And: “He will be condemned.” And: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Yet you, seduced by I do not know what rashness, press the contrary, saying that a human being outside the faith of Christ, in his paternal religion, which he believes he believes to be true and pleasing to God, or living innocently according to the law of nature, especially when perhaps he has never heard anything of the faith of Christ, is to be saved in his own confidence. Christ did not say this, but that whoever believes in the only-begotten Son of God will be saved, while whoever does not believe will be condemned. He excepted no one; he admitted no condition, for he had come to suffer for all, and by faith alone had provided for the salvation of all. If faith in the Savior is lacking, then no confidence will save the unbeliever. For the holy bishop Augustine said in On Faith to Peter: Hold most firmly, and do not doubt at all, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, heretics, and schismatics who end this present life outside the Catholic Church will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

Now you see where foolish compassion drags you: measuring divine things by human laws, so that you may make God merciful in all things, you do not fear to judge his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a liar. But Christ is truthful, who says that those who do not believe in him are to be damned; you, however, are rash and false, who hold that anyone can be saved outside his faith. Whoever truly believes in Christ does not permit anyone at all outside the unity of the Catholic Church of Christians to be called saved. Whoever says the contrary shows that he is not a true and good Christian.

For this is the inviolable judgment of Catholic tradition, which the Lord Jesus himself, the Son of God, defined in the holy Gospel: that no one is to be saved outside his faith, which he himself established, taught, and confirmed with his own blood. Therefore whoever affirms, or believes in his heart, that a man is to be saved in any sect whatever outside the faith of Jesus Christ, is not a good Christian, but rather an apostate and a disciple of Antichrist; with whom, unless he repents, he should know that he will be tormented forever in hell. For he is Antichrist, not a Christian, who says that one who does not believe in the Lord Jesus is to be saved without the Savior.

Therefore, most wise Caesar, let no one appear in the sight of your Majesty, let no one feel that you adhere to him, who thinks that men are to be saved outside the faith of Jesus Christ. For everyone who believes that someone is to be saved outside the faith of Christ has denied both Christ and his Gospel. But when we say that all who are not Christians are damned, this is not a mark of cruelty but of true piety. For it is better to believe the truth firmly than to agree falsely with a man. That all Jews, pagans, gentiles, Saracens, schismatics, heretics, and unbelievers are without doubt to be damned with the demons, the Church of the saints testifies; and it has taken up and confirmed this judgment from no other source than Christ's words. For thus he said: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; by this, good Christians are designated in faith and deed. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Here all Jews, pagans, Saracens, gentiles, and whoever do not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ are denoted.

Concerning schismatics and heretics, moreover, Christ's judgment is manifest in the Gospel when he says: Whoever refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican. Gentiles are pagans, and publicans are manifest and public sinners; of their damnation the most certain Church of the saints has no doubt. For who among Christians would doubt that gentiles and notorious sinners, manifest as such, are to be damned? Since, therefore, all schismatics and heretics despise the holy Church, they are most rightly said to be like gentiles and publicans, who are to be damned for their offenses and demerits; and with them they will justly undergo equal punishments of everlasting damnation. Behold how just a sentence of damnation Christ the Savior ...the sentence which the foolish compassion of men, not to say impious cruelty, presumes are to be saved. They desire to be merciful toward lost men, and they do not fear to show themselves cruel toward God. Those whom he, by justice, has assigned to death, these men assert, with the worst presumption, are to be recalled to life. It is neither good nor useful for a Christian, whether seriously or in jest, to contradict Christ. He is impious, not Christian, who says that any unbelievers are to be saved.

In Adam, the first man, when he fell, we all sinned, and the wrath of God remained upon the whole human race from the beginning of the world until Christ. Christ came, born of a virgin, God and man, innocent of sin; he voluntarily underwent the death of the cross, and, having been made mediator between God and man, removed the wrath of original guilt from those who believe in him. For thus he says, John 4: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.”

Indeed, without faith in Jesus Christ no one will be saved, however justly and holily he may seem to live in his own religion. For almighty God can save a believer without material baptism, but he cannot save one who denies without faith. No one is saved unwillingly, because no one believes except willingly. For the Lord knows those who are his, since he saves those who believe in the Son through repentance, but condemns unbelievers by the equity of justice.

Hence, with the way closed off, a new question has knocked at the mind: what should be thought concerning the infants and simple-minded persons of unbelieving pagans and Jews? To this one must answer briefly: just as the infants of Christians, baptized in the faith of their parents, are saved, so the unbaptized children of all unbelievers will be damned in the unbelief of their parents. The judgment concerning the simple-minded of each religion is similar: just as we believe without doubt that baptized simple-minded Christians are to be saved, so we say without doubt that those belonging to unbelievers are to be damned.

Again, it is asked here what is to be thought in a catholic manner about those men who inhabit the newly discovered islands in the great sea, of which there is no mention among the ancient cosmographers, and who, as we have been informed, have never heard anything at all about the Christian religion. A brief answer, conformable in all respects to the things written above, is given: because the truth has made absolutely no exception from damnation for anyone who does not believe, neither an islander, nor one not adjoining our world, nor anyone else, whether dwelling near or far away, but without distinction and without definition of persons, he concluded in a general saying: “He who believes and has been baptized shall be saved; but he who has not believed shall be condemned,” Mark 16, “and the wrath of God remains upon him.” Who removes the wrath of God from man except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mediator of God and men? 1 Timothy 2. By what means, except through faith formed in him who tasted death while innocent?

Since, therefore, no one is saved without faith, we cannot promise salvation to those ignorant of Christ, who, it is agreed, do not have faithful piety toward him. Accordingly, we must necessarily say that all are to be damned who do not believe in the Son of God, whether they have heard about him or are wholly ignorant of him. Yet we grant one thing: if any among those who are ignorant of Christ have lived well according to the law of nature, invoking one God, even if they have sometimes sinned, provided they performed repentance before death, they have been damned, or are to be damned, less severely than those who either hear of Christ and despise him, or have lived wickedly and basely among both groups. For God is just; he does injury to no one, but renders to each according to his works.

But the wrath of God remains upon everyone who does not believe in his only-begotten Son, because of the original sin of the first man, from which no one is justified except through faith and the baptism of the Lord and Savior. of our Savior Jesus Christ. Original sin, if it is present in a human being alone, as in little children, unless it is removed through Christ, condemns the one who has it only to the punishment of loss, by which he is forever barred from the vision of God and from the enjoyment of the blessedness of the saints. But an adult who sins mortally will be punished after death with a twofold punishment, namely of loss and of sense, so that he both does not see God and, feeling without end the pains of the fire of Gehenna, never escapes.

Moreover, Jews and Saracens, and all the rest who hear of the faith of Christ and despise it, are without doubt damned to both the punishment of loss and the punishment of sense, whether otherwise they live innocently according to the law of nature, or the contrary. But among those who have never had any hearing of Christ, if any lived innocently according to the law of nature up to death, I do not think that they have supplied a cause by which they should be said or believed to be damned to the punishment of sense, although they are forever deprived of the vision of God, which theologians have called the punishment of loss. For no one will behold the face of God the almighty Father unless he has been reborn through faith in Christ.

Now let us bring our judgment to a conclusion against those who, when we assert these things catholicly according to the doctrine of Christ, object with foolish reflection: Why did almighty God, since he is supremely good, will to create so many thousands of human beings whom from eternity he foreknew would be damned? For if a comparison of Christians is made with unbelievers, scarcely a twentieth part of the human beings of the whole world today believes in our Lord Jesus Christ. The immeasurable curiosity of this question has often struck many; if their faith in Christ were firm, and their devotion fervent in love of him, they would not seek such unusual and difficult things.

For what man of such great learning or holiness is found among mortals that, apart from God himself, he could disclose to us the cause of the divine will? For the cause of God’s will is incomprehensible, since he himself is the cause of his own most righteous will, the eternal, inviolable order; and, as I said above, God does injury to no one.

When God brought the universal flood upon the earth, were not only eight human beings saved in the ark, while all the rest perished in the inundation of waters? The cause of their perishing was sin; but that they were created had no other cause than the uncircumscribable goodness of God. That few were saved while many perished was a preceding figure, a mystery, and Noah’s ark was a sacrament of the Christian faith. For just as outside Noah’s ark all perished in the flood, so now all who are outside the unity of the catholic Church of Christians will without doubt perish eternally in their sins: Jews as much as pagans, heretics, and schismatics alike. The justice of God damns those whom his goodness created. But his mercy saves those whom grace has confirmed, because, as the holy Apostle says, “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” since he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Let us rightly weigh the freedom of the human will, and we shall know that the will of God is just.

¶ On the miracles of unbelievers. Question Three.

Question Third

Good Christians work miracles through public righteousness; evil Christians, through signs of public righteousness; but unbelievers through private contracts with demons, namely implicit or explicit ones. Concerning the good the Lord said in the holy Gospel: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak with new tongues, they shall take up serpents, and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them. They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.”

But concerning evil Christians who work miracles in the name of Jesus Christ, we read thus in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name done many mighty works? And then I will declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity.”

Outside the Church of God, however, where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is not invoked, if any marvels occur beyond the custom of nature or of human art, no good Christian doubts that they are done by the cooperation of demons. Your Caesar’s Serenity should therefore judge works of this kind to be called wonders rather than miracles, by a discernment of power. Nor does this judgment depart from the principle of truth, so that a necessary distinction may be maintained between prodigies of light and of darkness.

I find four producers of wonders, but I acknowledge one alone who truly works miracles in the principal sense: God, as the cause of all good things. Therefore the first and greatest producer of all wonders is God, who has filled and illumined the whole world with signs, miracles, and powers. None of the others is to be compared with him, who created heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them; who alone is almighty, just, holy and upright, good, incomprehensible, greatest, glorious, immense, and everlasting. All other things are beneath him, since whatever can happen wondrously in this world is certainly less than the whole world itself, which he was able to create out of nothing. Likewise every miracle that can be done through a human being is less than the human being himself, whom God, the creator of all things, formed from the beginning in his image and likeness.

And although the miracles of God in visible natures have now, among mortals, almost become commonplace through the constancy of seeing them, nevertheless, if we look upon them wisely, they will appear greater and rarer than all unusual things. Now the manner in which God works miracles is the unchangeable will of God, which, since it is almighty, does all things whatsoever it has willed in heaven and in heaven and on earth. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. The will of God is ordered and everlasting; therefore his miracles are incomparably greater than the rest. For greater than all the miracles of this world is the whole universe that we behold, and whatever is contained in it, created by the will of God. The unchangeable divine will, enduring, works all things, since it lacks both beginning and end. But whatever God wills, he always wills; because, since willing and being able are the same in him, it does not belong to the unchangeable one to labor.

Hence the creator of all things has displayed for both good and evil people all the universal miracles that he makes, so that they may be seen; and after the general ones, which have now become commonplace through use among mortals, he has also shown, in almost individual creatures, innumerable things especially worthy of wonder.

The second producer of miracles is the good angel, who very often works wonders among mortals both by natural power and by divine power. For those most blessed spirits are sent by divine ordinance into service for the faithful, Heb. 1, and they provide to both good and evil people the benefits that belong to nature; but to those alone who believe in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ they administer the gifts of saving grace. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which are done by invocation of the divine name in the Church of the saints are displayed through their ministry and cooperation.

But the wonders of unbelievers, if any are done today or are read to have been done formerly, are either fabricated or falsely claimed, or are accomplished by the deception of demons. For it cannot happen that any unbelievers work miracles by the ministry of good angels, since where Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is not believed in, no signs of grace are displayed through good spirits to impious and reprobate human beings. Indeed, since they are obstinate in the error of false religion, if they have attained anything miraculous in their own estimation, there is no doubt at all that it is done through the ministry of demons. For since they are wholly unlike the good angels, they obtain no familiarity with them.

No despiser of the Christian faith can please God; rather, whoever is proved to displease almighty God is without doubt deprived of the familiarity of the holy angels. Yet by this we do not deny that every human being is entrusted to some good spirit, by whose ministry, even if he is an unbeliever in the Son of God, he receives the benefits of nature, although he does not reach the gifts of grace. But to those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, they confer not only the benefits of nature, but also administer the gifts of grace.

...they minister. It is therefore clear that if any miracles occur among unbelievers, they could not occur by God’s gift or by the ministry of the holy angels, since all such people are placed outside the unity of the Church, and signs cannot be worked by the impious through public righteousness. For God, as has been said, does not remove his original wrath from a person except through faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is unbelieving toward the Son of God will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. John 3.

Therefore everyone upon whom the wrath of God remains cannot please God; and so, if any wonders are done at his prayers, they should be believed to have been performed not by God’s power nor by the ministry of angels, but rather by the agency of demons. The third worker of wonders is the devil, who, like an ape, longs to imitate whatever he sees; and he deceives the minds of men, especially unbelievers, with various illusions, and seduces those who believe him by a certain likeness of miracles. For I do not judge it difficult for demons to be able to delude the senses of men, since it is agreed that by nature they were created subtler than all mortals. But they cannot know the thoughts of mortals except by a kind of conjecture, namely when we make our inward things manifest by certain signs. Demons foretell future things, and sometimes speak truths, sometimes they are deceived in their conjectures, and they deceive others. From the beginning of the world they have known certain signs that precede events, and by experience and practice with these they sometimes foretell truly what is going to happen; for when they have seen the signs known to them that precede an event, they at once conjecture what is in a person’s thought. Yet they very often deceive, because they themselves are deceived.

For when they are questioned about some matter that they do not know, for example whether or on what day a messenger sent far away will soon return, in the blink of an eye they immediately reach the place where they know him to be. When they see that he has already begun the journey back, they carefully count the day’s stages; and, returning at once to the questioner, they affirm that the absent man will certainly come on a fixed day. But if he either delays on the road or turns aside for other reasons, then the demons, deceived in their own judgment, must necessarily be wrong.

They gladly involve themselves in predictions, and they are quite ready to foretell future things to human beings for the sake of honor and esteem, because they especially desire to be regarded as worthy of admiration. They seek divine honors and greatly desire to be feared by mortals. Just as boys hiding in a secret place or running about in masks suddenly burst out from their hiding places and shake with unexpected terror their companions who suspect nothing of the sort, and then hide themselves again so as not to be recognized, and when they see the unknowing ones terrified they boast, as though they seemed to have gained great honor from this; after their example certain demons, more closely bound to the earth and very restless in their dealings around human beings, whom the ancients called bacucei, frighten people at night and seek nothing more from mortals than the esteem of divinity.

Hence also, in the presence of those before whom they are permitted to appear in some likeness, they sometimes perform various delusions; and they show themselves as terrifying in people’s minds, as occasion allows, whenever they can. They gladly take on the likeness of a human body, but they do not always find suitable airy matter with which to clothe themselves. Therefore they quite often appear monstrous and horrible, because they have not had suitable humors or vapors for the perfection of the appearance they wanted.

Moreover, the more they are bound to earthly substances, the duller they have become through the accident of matter. Hence, because of the ignorance they contracted through disobedience, the predictions of demons are frequently false, although by divine permission they are sometimes also verified. For, as that most holy John Chrysostom... he says: It is granted to the devil sometimes to speak the truth, so that he may commend his lie by a rare truth; for if he never spoke the truth, he could deceive no one, and his deception would by no means suffice for tempting. It is therefore no wonder if demons sometimes seem to foretell true things to unbelieving people, since they were once able to offer prophecies among the Gentiles in idols. Nor is it any wonder if they sometimes provide treatment for the sick, since they know the natures of all herbs and can very easily apply them to the sick, either removing diseases which they had previously inflicted, or withdrawing for a time from the senses those which they inflict by their causes.

For almighty God, by the right of the imperial majesty of the universe, uses even the ministry of demons, both for the testing of the faithful and for the punishment of the impious. Since they are perverted in affection, obstinate and proud in their rebellion, they greatly desire divine esteem and honors; and therefore they gladly answer the invocations of unbelievers, which they are accustomed to pour out to their gods, as though they themselves were gods. They also seem among unbelievers to raise the dead to life, and they show wonders to curious people, so that, confirmed by miracles, they may render them altogether obstinate in their former error. But they do not truly raise the dead, ## Question Three

but deceive human senses in various ways. For either they themselves enter the corpses of the dead and carry them about for a time as though alive, or, after these have been taken away to a more remote place, they present to the onlookers for viewing some likeness in the appearance of the life of the deceased, as the experience of certain people has informed us.

We believe it is clear that demons can show, in a certain false likeness, everything whatever that the saints do as miracles in truth. All the miracles of demons are either phantasms or things done by a certain natural skill. For if human beings experienced in the more hidden mysteries of nature, by a certain application of matter to form that is concealed from others, produce unusual and wondrous effects, such as forming natural eels from the dew of heaven, bees from calves’ flesh, serpents from certain roots of herbs, and many things like these, not to mention greater things, as experiment has made us tested in many cases, who will deny that demons, of subtler nature and greater experience, can perform more wonders of natural things which are evident to no human being?

But the fourth worker of miracles is the human being, who works wonders in four ways, which to those who know neither the cause nor the manner do not seem human. And first, indeed, by invocation of the divine name, when the merit of accepted holiness joins with faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. In this way the holy apostles and their imitators, by the power of God together with the merit of holiness in the unity of faith, performed miracles. But unbelievers cannot perform miracles in this way, since they do not walk the necessary path of faith toward salvation. For even though very many of them believe in God, nevertheless, because they refuse to believe in the mediator of God and human beings, they have gone very far away from God’s mercy.

But all things, as the holy Gospel promises, are possible for those who believe in God and our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, for those who adorn right faith also with holy works. Indeed, just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so also faith without works is dead. For almighty God would grant us everything that we ask in the faith of Christ, if we did everything according to the faith that we owe. Believe firmly, and act faithfully, and you will always obtain everything.

Second, a human being performs miracles through likeness to angelic purity. For the more our mind, confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ, becomes purer through love, the more, having been made like the holy angels, it will attain greater familiarity with them. Whoever, however, has obtained complete familiarity with the holy angels ...familiarity, he will, whenever he wishes, shine forth in miracles, by God’s gift. For the holy angels reveal to pure men who are fervent in the love of God secrets hidden from others, and by command of the Creator they make many things manifest to them. For the Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth. The Lord will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them. For whoever is united with Christ through grace is refreshed by the frequent visitation of angels; and often, when necessity demands, he is made illustrious by signs and powers through their ministry.

This is why those oppressed by various illnesses also betake themselves to the aid of the saints; and, turning over in their minds the promises of the Lord, they obtain by the merits of others what they cannot obtain by their own. Their holy devotion in the faith of Christ receives salvation from the Lord, because, aided by the purity of their own conscience and supported by the merit of another’s holiness, it rises, not rashly, in sure hope.

Miracles are done in the Church of God by divine power in a threefold respect or means. For sometimes Almighty God works a miracle through the ministry of angels solely by the merits of the worker himself, just as Saint Martin healed a blind man and a lame man against their will. Sometimes miracles are done solely by the merit of the sufferer, as we read that many were cured by bad Christians whom the sick believed to be very good in the faith. Third, there is no doubt that healings of this kind are done by the merit of both, namely of the sufferer and of the worker together, as Christ says to someone in the holy Gospel: “If you can believe, all things are possible to the one who believes.” For faith is required for a miracle to such a degree that our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into his own country, marveled because he could not do any mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things takes place among unbelievers, where neither holiness is found in the worker nor orthodox faith in the sufferer.

Third, therefore, man works miracles through the cooperation of diabolical wickedness as an intermediary. And this can happen in three ways: namely by manifest invocation of demons, by implication, and by supposition. By manifest invocation, necromancers and little women whom we commonly call witches do wondrous things; through likeness of depraved will they have passed into fellowship with demons. For just as in the Church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the spirit of holiness, so in the school of demons certain characters and modes of invocation are marks of a pact between a man and a malignant spirit.

Hence, when signs of demons are presented through works of witchcraft, malignant spirits, once invoked, are accustomed to appear willingly and to display both horrible works of witchcraft and certain wonders. But witches and necromancers produce wondrous effects by invocation of demons in different ways. Witches are subject to demons by a certain kind of profession; by their ministry they disturb the air, raise storms, devastate crops, and make men and beasts ill. They carry on foul commerce of the filthiest pleasure with demons, and by pernicious spells they call back from the lower world into sight whomever they wish. Their deeds should not be called miracles, but rather works of witchcraft, and they deservedly ought to be punished by the ultimate penalty.

Necromancers, however, subject themselves to demons not by manifest profession, but by an implicit condition, when they claim that they compel them to appear visibly in a circle not only by conjurations and the display of characters, but also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are infinite, since they all manifestly conspire into fellowship with demons, whether implicitly or explicitly. Although necromancers are not all equal either in art or in deed, nevertheless to their own destruction and damnation... they are all agreed in damnable curiosity, by which they desire, through the support of demons, to obtain what they cannot discover naturally. All their works and volumes are full of superstitions and impiety, and for this reason they must be banished far from the borders of believers.

There is a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers in the East, who by their illusions miserably deceive the human race, and long ago turned almost all Asia, both Greater and Lesser, away from the faith of Christ. Illusions can be produced in three ways: by the ministry of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian will doubt that the miracles of unbelievers occur in one of these ways, when the definite root of the worker is established.

Today, moreover, there are many among Christians who are devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, witches, and men reprobate concerning the faith, who deceive many by excessive curiosity and promise impossibilities by their arts. But by the involvement of demons wondrous things sometimes occur, whenever, that is, a man not sufficiently and rightly grounded in the faith does or desires something other than befits a Christian, even if he does not believe it to be any sin; and although this ought not to happen, nevertheless the devil, intruding himself, often supplies the desired effect.

Such is that which those suffering from spasms commonly use. On the sacred day of Parasceve they make a ring of any metal during the office, and afterward always wear it on the heart-finger. These things are utterly vain and have no root of truth at all. Yet I cannot deny that I have seen certain people cured of spasm by this same vanity. Likewise, I know that certain very strong locks have been opened by words and herbs, which I do not think was done either by the power of God or by the force of the things applied.

I could introduce innumerable similar things that I have seen and heard; what else are their manifest effects but certain miracles of demons? Finally, there are some excessively curious people who stubbornly place faith and confidence in characters, slips of paper, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, and often obtain wondrous effects. We do not doubt in the least that the devil has supplied these, not by the merit of holiness nor by the mercy granted by God, but rather by faithless credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, readily come to the vain operations of the impious in order to destroy the souls of mortals. For what else are characters and interpretations of hidden names but certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever places faith in characters promising wondrous effects has implicitly denied the faith of Christ and the church of the saints.

Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to spare their betters, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions; and in these implicit pacts with demons are equated, to the dishonor of the Christian faith and to their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied excessively among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and handed them over into the power of a faithless people, so that they may feel them as exactors of punishments, since by imitation they served persistently not the living and true God, but vain superstitions.

Moreover, we shall clearly recognize that wondrous things are done by the substitution of demons, if we inquire into the truth more carefully. Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in our God Jesus Christ, if they perform any miracles, we believe these are done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by the merit of holiness, but by the substitution of demons. For whenever they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for the mercy of some wondrous effect, the devil, knowing that because there is no salvation for sinners, and because the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, secretly presents himself in place of the God who has been invoked; and, if he can, with the Lord permitting it, he grants to their prayers what is requested. The devil uses this substitution all the more freely insofar as he is less hindered by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son; and they are in the power of the devil, and therefore he thrusts himself upon those who invoke him in place of God. Hence, blinded in their errors, they invoke God, in whose Son they do not believe; and when he disdains to hear them while they remain under wrath, the devil, the false worker of miracles, comes near. Thus they believe the devil’s mockeries, who scorn to believe the true miracles of God. From demons they receive false miracles suited to their errors, because they have refused to believe the truth, that is, Christ. For there are many among those unbelievers who worship one God, the creator of all things, do not adore idols, and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they scorn to believe the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them; and they vanish away in their follies, thinking God near to them, while in those things in which they do not believe rightly, they are subjected to demons. Therefore, putting faith in false miracles, they are confirmed in their errors by a lie. It may not be irksome to introduce, O Caesar, a likeness of this matter. There was a certain man, a keeper of swine, who had enclosed in a staff a little written sheet containing the name of the blessed martyr Blasius. He placed so much faith in it that, when the staff was fixed in the ground in the middle of the herd, he believed every wolf was prevented from approaching. When this foolish confidence had at length been strengthened by long experience, the man went securely wherever he wished, leaving the swine in the wood without danger, since no wolf now had access to them. It happened that a passerby saw this in the shepherd’s absence; and, perceiving that a demon had charge of guarding the herd, he said to him: “What are you doing here, wretched one?” He answered: “I am guarding these swine.” The other said: “Who entrusted the care of the swine to you?” Again he answered: “The foolish confidence of the shepherd. For he thinks that a certain little sheet enclosed in the staff is of great power, by which, through the merits of some Blasius, wolves are kept away from the swine. But he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities. Therefore, since the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his swine and willingly substitute myself for Blasius.” Thus, he said, mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that unless we wish to lose our reputation and honor among them, it is altogether necessary that we very often come to the aid of their foolish invocations. By a likeness of this fact demons deceive miserable unbelievers, and the miracles that they ask of God in prayer are often obtained by the substitution of the more malign spirits. For in those things that concern the worship or honor of God, demons gladly thrust themselves in; and those who cannot obtain manifest honors are, of course, delighted by hidden ones. At the same time it should be noted that from the beginning of the world miracles of outstanding excellence have never been lacking to any religion or sect, although they have not all been done from one principle. For whatever miracles were done in the true religion were done from no other source than God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had them; and now grace also has them. Almighty God, who gave religion, himself also works miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, it is not God but the devil who works them. For since God is truth, he did not establish false religions; and therefore he has never adorned a lie with his miracles. Muhammad, who, filled with an evil demon, established a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of error also gave the miracle, when permission was secretly received from [unclear]. he could display a false one to the deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Muhammad as he was persuading an uncultivated people to a new religion, perhaps no one would have put faith in him. For he too, both by the subtlety of his intellect and by the cooperation of the devil, showed certain wonders to the peoples, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine also by new miracles.

Miracles were not lacking even to pagan idolaters, if we do not deny the histories. The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illumined by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been made void, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if they perform any wonders today, they are the works of demons and manifest signs of error.

For demons keep watch with the greatest zeal so that those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they may, by continuing their fraud, make obstinate in error even unto death. Indeed, when God for just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unrecognized; and, when he sees that salvation is far away, by false miracles he seduces the minds of the ignorant as though he were the Lord present, that is, as though he were the Lord, and seduces the minds of the ignorant. Therefore whatever miracles belong to unbelievers are the works of demons, because, just as there is no salvation for mortals outside the unity of the Christian faith, so without Christ the most holy power of wonders is not granted. For now demons, lying hidden in ambush, long since defeated and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the incarnation of the Lord; and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also some who add a fourth to the three modes set forth above, saying that the mind, or the spirit of the human being itself, can naturally perform wonders, provided that it knows how to recall itself from every adventitious thing back into itself, above sense, into unity. For those who assert such things promise to do wonders of nature, to predict the future, to disclose people’s secrets, to remove diseases, and suddenly to change people’s plans. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, which I have not experienced, it is necessary that something of an external power should now intervene, and that either a good angel or a malignant spirit should occupy the one thinking in some part. But if none of the external powers mingles itself in, the one prophesying must form the principle of his speaking either from conjectures or from bold presumption, and must pronounce a judgment sometimes true and sometimes false. Indeed, as long as the spirit is engaged in the body, it naturally understands nothing without the ministry of sense. Hence I would not wholly oppose them if they grant that our confused and unformed intellect is aided by an equal ministry.

For we see among those who, contemplating the measure of the flesh, often pass beyond themselves because of an inner love and desire for Jesus, that they are lifted upward from the earth into the air; and we think that they exceed bodily weight not merely by their own keenness of mind, but also by divine power. Therefore the three principles of the aforementioned opinion, unknown to many, in my judgment satisfy few, namely, that the mind, while placed in the body, should by its own power produce wonderful effects outside itself.

For what then? Let anyone ignorant of nature tell me whether bodily weight can be lightened by the operation of the mind. With two men bearing witness together with me, I report a thing experienced. When I was pursuing the studies of letters as a youth, one night four of us were sleeping in one bed. A contemporary of mine rose from my side while asleep, as he was accustomed to do, and, with his eyes closed and the fifteenth-day moon shining in, walked about through the whole house as though awake. He climbed walls and surpassed the agility of cats. He also ascended the roof easily and [unclear] Still asleep, he crossed over; he stepped on all of us with his feet, and we felt his weight no more than if a tiny mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, all the fastenings of the doors immediately opened of their own accord. He passed through the higher parts of the house with the greatest speed, and, like a sparrow, clung to the roofs.

I speak of things seen, not heard by vague report. These seem to be offices of the soul, not of the body; by its natural power, so to speak, it uses them almost freely when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling-place of the body. But since this matter is not in every respect suited to the question proposed, let us defer the treatment of the causes of these marvels to another time. For we do not think such things marvelous to the wise, who have very well understood the power and nobility of the human mind, since, hindered only by the interposition of the body, it is in some respect judged equal to the angels.

Finally, we pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which a frenzied person works very threatening effects upon external things. The imagination of one who is most strongly confident can also do much toward producing marvelous effects, whether it is directed toward a true object or toward an object merely supposed. Hence, since there are so many kinds and modes of working wonders, it is not surprising if Jews, Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and the rest who are placed outside the faith of Christ, whatever unbelievers they may be, since they cannot perform miracles by public righteousness, carry out marvels either by the assistance of demons or by artful industry.

Nor does it escape me that by the same reasoning the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as though they were done not by the power of the Creator, but rather by the involvement or supposition of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that all the miracles of unbelievers are accomplished through the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and obstinately thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture.

Question Four

Question Fourth

The fourth question of your most serene Majesty was this: Why did almighty God not give sacred Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith, of the New Testament as well as the Old, open, manifest, uniform in all things, and plainly sufficient for all things, but rather wrapped up, and in many places full of enigmas? For many things are necessary for the more perfect understanding of the faith which are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures.

To this most sacred question of your Majesty it seems one must reply: Every Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity, foreordained before all time, written in time, in no other way than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. All the works of God are perfect; and therefore, since the Scripture of which we are speaking is a work of God, it is necessary to confess it perfect in all things.

For God, the supreme judge, whose works are all perfect, bestowed upon his Scriptures, in order, what he willed and as he willed; and he undoubtedly infused them into those receiving them, so that they might be written in due measure. Almighty God bestowed such authority and majesty upon sacred Scripture that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended by human speech.

Therefore divine Scripture, which on the surface of its verses may appear confused to the unlearned, seems manifest to those who understand it; and unless one reads it by that Spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into men, one by no means arrives at its very understanding. Otherwise The learned man who burns under the cover of the flesh and with vain desires reads it in one way; the man whom the love of God truly inflames, stripped of pleasures, understands it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men who think carnally do not understand the divine Scriptures, since, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, they have never perceived the sweetness of the Spirit of God.

It is just as if you were to show to a boy learning the first elements of letters some written volume whose script was unlike that of his own little book: when he could not read it, he would at once cry out that the writing was bad and not properly formed. In the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures while thinking only carnally, and who do not grasp the things that belong to the divine Spirit, weighed down by vices and rashness, although they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach the holy Scriptures because they do not understand them.

For it is not lawful for everyone indiscriminately to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast that touches the mountain be overwhelmed with stones. Now many arise, in a perverse order, who have spent the whole time of their life on humane letters, and when they have become old men, by wrongly interpreting the divine Scriptures which they have never learned, they do not explain them but confound them, and discuss them according to their own sense. From this comes the fact that whoever do not understand the sacred Scriptures in the Spirit by which they were infused into those who wrote them have the veil of ignorance and rashness spread over their hearts, in the manner of the Jews, and very often draw from them the poison of pernicious error, from which the humble, approaching in the Spirit of God, have received the cup of salvation.

For heavenly doctrine is not found in the words of Scripture, but in its meaning; not on the surface of its expressions, but in the understanding; not in the leaves of ornate speech, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence the divine pope Gregory says: “Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in its manner of speaking, since in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it discloses a hidden mystery; and just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has in public what may nourish little ones, and it preserves in secret what may suspend the minds of the exalted in admiration of its sweetness, like a certain wonderful river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim.”

And Saint Augustine says on Genesis: “Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it laughs at the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its virtue it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones.” Greater indeed is the authority of sacred Scripture than all the perspicacity of human intellect. Therefore, in order that one may come to their true understanding, the mind must first be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the aid of divine goodness must be earnestly implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illumine the understanding of the learner. For to the authority of the divine Scriptures the necks of all powers must be submitted.

And as the divine Jerome says: “One must never flatter a man in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected; for in both Testaments it is wholly true in the narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terribly to be feared in its threats.”

For this reason it has not been granted to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but it is permitted only to those to whom both love gives continuity of study and the Spirit of God grants true understanding in purified minds. But whoever is befouled by the darkness of vices, whoever walks proudly with a swollen mind, whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God either in part or in whole, should never trust that he can attain to understanding them. For the authority of Scripture itself says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” Ours is the slowness It is the slowness of our intelligence and the impurity of our desire whenever we do not understand the divine Scriptures rightly, since the veil of pernicious occupation remains spread over our hearts and does not allow us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the meaning which the Holy Spirit infused into the divine Scriptures, but, grasping the bare words of the writers, twist them into another meaning.

Indeed, if our minds were cleansed of carnal vices; if, through the continual practice of sobriety, our intelligence were exercised in the Scriptures; if faith and reverence were shown to the holy Scriptures as their dignity requires, every diligent student would understand more clearly than light that there is nothing confused in the sacred readings, nothing discordant, nothing unfitting, nothing absurd, or inserted without the most just reason.

For all the passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; and whenever anything in them seems to be set down obscurely, it was done by divine providence, so that the studious mind might have the necessary exercise of devotion, and the faith of the simple might not lose its place of due reverence. Therefore it was not by chance, but by everlasting providence, that God wished the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that they might abound in as many mysteries as there are meanings to be explained in a Catholic manner by teachers under the inspiration of the Spirit of God. For, as Saint Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it brings forth many statements of truth and produces them into the light for human beings; for when one person draws out this meaning, and another draws out another, in expounding it in a Catholic manner, it becomes known how high and profound Scripture is.

Therefore let no man swollen with secular learning suppose that he understands sacred Scripture unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning is of more value for exercising the intelligence than for enlightening the understanding toward true wisdom.

Thus without doubt divine Scripture is clear and manifest to minds purified through continual exercise of the fear of God and frequent study of reading; yet to the filthy and to those puffed up with secular wisdom it seems confused and obscure.
