Therefore the man who understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly is the one who, with purified affection and frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote them. For if they read in a spirit other than that by which the Scriptures are believed to have been inspired so that they might be written, the mind must necessarily be wholly shut away from true understanding.

But when we encounter some dissonance in them, let us understand that it belongs only to the words, not to the meanings; and that these things arise not by chance, but by the providence of God and in orderly fashion, so that the mind, exercised in the Scriptures, may be strengthened for a longer time and not grow wholly sluggish.

For God’s counsel cannot be deceived; but since the divine Scriptures were written according to the counsel of his will, it necessarily follows that they are true and in no way false. They were human beings by whom the divine Scriptures were handed down to us; certainly they wrote words used according to human custom, by which they might signify to posterity what that supreme excellence of divinity wished to be known to mortals.

Therefore you now, who are devoted to secular wisdom and attack the divine Scriptures, say this: from where do you believe the Church received the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which it has accepted and venerates as true, authoritative, and holy Christian Scripture? From God, or from human beings? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks Scripture which he believes to have been inspired by God very plainly resists divine ordinance. But if it is from human beings, why do you hope for the eternal salvation promised in it, which a human being cannot give?

Unless perhaps, in your madness, you go on to say that all things are inventions, and that nothing remains after death except ashes, and that the mind undergoes destruction together with the body; such a profession would show you to be no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, If you believe, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if, having fallen with apostates into a reprobate mind, you say that they were composed by human beings, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness.

You openly show yourselves to be ignorant and rash judges, since you condemn a Scripture that you do not understand. Truly, because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind any longer against the rashness of the unskilled. This one thing I want you to know: no one understands unless he receives; but because you place the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, you therefore do not have the true understanding of wisdom.

Almighty and eternal God deigns, as enlightener, to be present by grace to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except God. To them the Spirit of God brings help by his presence, those whom he has found rooted in the love of truth; and, once they have been purified from every foreign thing, he leads them into the knowledge of all things.

For truly, to those who love God, all things are open, all things bare, all things manifest; for whoever, through love, beholds in the faith of Jesus Christ the one who creates and governs all things, knows all things that are necessary for his salvation.

But on the contrary, the enlightenment of God dwells very far from the slothful, the wicked, gluttons, the envious, the greedy, those given to concubinage, the filthy, the lustful, murderers, the impious, the proud, and those alien to piety, leaving them to the judgment of the avenging demon, who, driving in the sharp point of savage fire, afflicts the senses and the mind, and arms and drives the impious still more toward committing crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also be liable to a harsher punishment.

Hence those entangled in vices, desires, and worldly things not only cannot penetrate the divine Scriptures by understanding, but, neglecting even themselves, they do not know themselves. Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is the perfect work of God, Caesar, we must so strengthen the mind that we believe it to be true, right, whole, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith.

Indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect in all things, and whole, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Therefore every Christian must take the greatest care that, by examining the divine Scriptures more than is fitting, he not overstep the boundaries of piety, because the author of Scripture is not a human being, but the Holy Spirit; and whoever struggles against the integrity of the Scriptures of God is convicted of resisting his ordinance.

Now Scripture, by the ordinance of God, is usefully woven together with parables, riddles, likenesses, and comparisons of figures, so that readers may be exercised toward understanding, and, once its inner sweetness has been tasted, the mind may be strengthened toward piety. And so, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of the Scriptures and not merely to the words, we shall understand that all things have been ordered rightly and properly.

For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which the knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so common and manifest as to be understood everywhere by all, since it is set forth to be understood only by the good and holy, not by evil, filthy, and polluted minds. For hence it is written: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” What is designated here by the beast, unless human beings who live in the manner of brute animals, without the love of God, in the pleasures of the flesh? And what is expressed by the mountain, unless the height of the divine Scriptures? When a beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a human being impure in mind, or weak in faith, who strives to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a teacher handing it down, [unclear] with various and pernicious [unclear].

He is wounded by errors of this kind as though by blows of stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane. Timothy 6. God therefore placed his hiding place in the height of the Scriptures, Psalm 17, which is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that it nevertheless always lies plainly open to the saints.

But why did almighty God not give holy Scripture as sufficient and manifest for everything that concerns the Christian faith? We answer briefly: there are two things which the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith, namely the Church and Scripture, so that what is not expressed clearly enough in the one may be declared more fully by the other. Hence, if we find anything in the holy Scriptures expressed less sufficiently concerning the rules of faith, we at once have recourse to the Church; and where the Church has need of saving instruction for piety, it immediately turns to Scripture. From this it follows that neither would the Church have authority without Scripture, nor Scripture faith without the Church, so that from the two one judgment may be made.

For Augustine says: “I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me.” But John Gerson says: “I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me.” Moreover, the holy Scripture confirms the Church, and it in like manner is confirmed by Scripture. The Church abounds whenever Scripture is lacking; and if the Church has any doubt, it returns to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God, who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ, the very same almighty one who alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord which is not easily broken, where divine Scripture through the Holy Spirit is joined to the authority of the Church, to such an extent that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church.

And so, O Caesar, it seems to me that we have assigned a sufficient reason, for your unconquered Majesty, for the question proposed: because if all things that concern the piety of faith were clearly expressed in the holy Scriptures, then our chosen mother Church would not possess so great an authority, and the merit of saving obedience would be emptied out in large part. At the same time, I think that enough has been answered for the principal question, where certain people judge sacred Scripture to be confused and tangled in very many places. Yet if they read it with due purity of mind, they would certainly find it perfect and solid.

Great is the authority of the catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning those things that regard the faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures, and to which the necks of all powers must be subjected. If anyone departs from its definition with rash daring, he has denied the Gospel of Christ. The congregation of the faithful, the holy Church, mother of Christians, is one; outside its unity no one will be saved. And although it may at times seem weak in morals, nevertheless, with the piety of Christ preserved, it has always remained constant in faith and has never erred.

On the Reprobate and Maleficent

Question Five

Your fifth question, most serene Highness, was this: why impious, evil, and reprobate people with respect to the faith, such as those women whom we commonly call witches, are able to command malignant spirits, while good men and most zealous observers of the Christian faith cannot command even good spirits, nor always malignant ones? I remember having answered this question some time ago in this way.

In all the works of the divine Majesty there is a sequence and order of beauty, of immovable equity, by which individual things, suitably disposed, remain in the rank they have received. For without its proper order nothing subsists in the world. In this order, the freedom of the will, which the Creator of all gave to human beings, cannot, by any violence of a power compelling it, be prevented from remaining remain in the order that the first human being received from the beginning of his creation. Hence no one among mortals is good except by the counsel of his own will, aided by the grace of the merciful God; and no one is evil except by his own accord, deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin. By uprightness of will we are made like the good spirits, if by holy and necessary works we prove the piety of the faith that we have in Christ. And just as the consummation of a good will makes good people equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious makes them like demons. Hence evil and perverse people, the more they have been depraved by the malice of their own will, become so much the more like demons in affection.

Through likeness, moreover, the familiarity of friendship is introduced, from which mutual confidence is gradually generated. From the confidence of the lesser in the greater arises command, whether it is true or simulated by cunning. Therefore, if wicked people seem to have any command over demons, it arises from the greatness of their depravity: namely, when their affection is so far depraved, and by a reprobate will they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons that join with them. For demons are not all equal in malice or in intelligence; rather, one is much craftier than another in quickness of understanding, and far worse in depraved affection. For those who, falling from their high seats, are more closely joined to the earth and inhabit caves and caverns are certainly duller than the others, to such a degree that they fear swords and rods, and seem to be moved by the threats of men who terrify them, as may be observed in those whom we call the possessed. But the demons who dwell farther away from the earth are subtler by nature and meet with human beings more rarely.

People full of malice, however, the more they advance in perversity of will, become so much the more like demons. Once admitted by them into familiarity, they then become bold, and receive over the demons whose familiarity they enjoy a command not of violent power, but of feigned simulation. For demons, in order to keep those people whom they have once received into surrender voluntary in their depravity, gladly subject themselves to them, as though moved by a simulated domination, and what they do willingly they pretend to do as though compelled to obedience. Indeed, no one obtains true command over demons unless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, has made him acceptable and dear to God. Thus, concerning those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus, Scripture says: “And he gave them power over all demons.” Therefore evil people command demons: people whom malevolence has made like them, likeness has made familiar to them, and familiarity has made their own and subject to them. It is as if, with a great prince, as often happens, some servant born in a humble station, joined to him by long familiarity, is said to command him, because he obtains from him, without contradiction, everything he has asked for, so that he seems more to rule his lord than to be ruled by him.

In accordance with this likeness, evil and reprobate people, who are admitted by demons into heartfelt familiarity and become very bold through prolonged confidence, receive over them a simulated, not to say familiar, command, which they have merited by likeness of a most depraved will. Hence whatever they request from demons who join with them by an agreement, whether implicit or explicit, they receive, unless at times, by divine ordinance, the demons are forbidden and cannot provide what is asked. Yet they do not everywhere join in this way with all reprobate and evil people, but only with those with whom, through the intervention of some compact, they have entered into covenants: such as witches, who have rendered homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom in common usage we call necromancers.

... whom the common people call necromancers.

There are two kinds of men who can lawfully command demons. The first is that of those men who, beloved by God through the merit of holiness, have received from him the power to trample the head of the ancient serpent, such as in the primitive Church were the apostles and their followers and disciples, of whom the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they shall cast out demons,” and “they shall take up serpents.”

The second kind is that of those men to whom, by reason of their order in the Church of God, it is granted to drive demons from human bodies by the power of the ministry they have received. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God when, that is, they are ordained by the bishop.

Again, there are two kinds of men who desire to command demons; and the utterly wicked conditions they accept show how unlawfully they presume to do so. The first and most pernicious kind is that of witches, who enter into pacts with demons and, after making a solemn profession, hand themselves over to some demon as his property and for perpetual service. What great evils this most pernicious kind of human beings commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, no one can express.

For first of all, denying God, the faith of Christ, and sacred baptism, they offer themselves in mind and body to demons; by their witchcraft they sicken, harm, and kill men and livestock. There is no disease which, God permitting, they cannot bring on, because, when in observance of the covenanted pact they present themselves as servants to demons, by alliance with them they dare whatever they wish.

Therefore they are not to be tolerated anywhere, but rather are to be utterly exterminated in every place, as God the creator of all commands: “You shall not suffer witches to live.” Some witches summon demons by spells; others entice them by prayers and sacrifices; the rest, provoking them by unspeakable acts and ceremonies, draw them into the service of their impiety.

It is therefore no wonder that witches seem to command demons, to whom they have become like through the impiety of a perverse will, and with whom they are in harmony through mutual association for the harm of the human race.

The second kind of depraved men who desire to command demons is that of those whom we commonly call necromancers. They profess arts full of execrations, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them openly visible, enclosed in a crystal or some other vessel. These most pernicious men, full of lying and superstition, commit such great evils that no good person could imagine them. For, in order to entice demons into obedience to themselves, they generally use the most shameful sacrifices and enter into an explicit pact with them.

They carry about many varied little books full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, falsely inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and wise men; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious people and drag them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise great and almost incredible things, and by hearing these things men are deceitfully held suspended in wonder.

They say that by rings, pentacles, images, exorcisms, and conjurations they can compel malignant demons to appear visibly in a circle, or in a crystal, or in some other receptacle, and to answer distinctly all questions put to them. Indeed all of them promise this, but in our times very few are found to whom malignant spirits, even evil ones, are obedient in this way, since God, by a most just reason, does not permit it, lest the curiosity of men, prone to novelties, after despising the religion of Christ...

...would seek aid from demons in time of need. But all those whom malignant spirits obey when summoned by the conjurations of necromancers have without doubt passed into their fellowship through an explicit or implicit pact. The number of the rest, however, is greater: those whom malignant spirits disdain to obey, although they are not afraid to occupy themselves at all times with the profane arts of necromancers.

And because, especially in our times, iniquity has begun to abound and the charity of many has grown cold, these accursed and most deceitful men have become very powerful. Although they are despised by demons, nevertheless, persisting in their pernicious doctrines, they deceive many. Believe me, Caesar, this most deceitful class of men is very harmful to your holy empire, and therefore, no less than the brood of witches, must be utterly exterminated.

They promise great things, and they lie in everything. Indeed, all the things promised in their books are empty and false, and they provide those who believe them nothing except tricks, frauds, and the most subtle deceptions. But if at times they seem to produce what they have promised, it should be clear to everyone that this happens only through the cooperation of demons, from whose fellowship one must flee no less than from the most savage torments of hell. For demons very often attend these necromantic operations, and, in order to keep their invokers obstinate in the treachery they have begun, they grant them what they ask, if they can. Yet sometimes, when summoned by conjurations, they disdain to appear, and nevertheless they have led away the minds of those who invoke them.

There is also another kind of men, no less foolish than superstitious: those, namely, who do not wish to have any commerce with demons, and nevertheless use in their vain operations things assigned to demons and, for that reason, wholly illicit. For they think that there is great and hidden power in characters, and therefore they commit various errors against the faith of Christ. But since this is not the time to recount their madness, let us pursue our subject.

Why good and just men do not obtain command over demons must now be stated briefly. Just as likeness of wills makes evil and impious men peers of demons, so unlikeness of wills renders good and just men wholly opposed to them. Between opposites and those unlike one another there can be no familiar association; rather, continual opposition and hatred prevail. But where no familiarity contracted through likeness of wills is found, there can be neither confidence of one toward another nor a mutual marvelous concurrence in operation. Nor do you, glorious Caesar, a man who are a great ruler and prince of men, admit as familiar to yourself anyone wholly contrary and unlike you in morals and continually resisting your will.

Good and upright men, because they always oppose the most depraved will of demons, can in no way pass into their fellowship, since they neither wish nor consent to be familiar with them, but with all their strength flee from and detest encounter with them. Therefore they do not obtain over them that fictitious command of which we have spoken. For no familiarity is secure unless likeness of wills has preceded it; nor can there be harmony between opposites, nor friendship between those of unlike will.

Nor do demons everywhere obey all evil and reprobate people, but only those whom they have bound to themselves by pacts and services; and when invoked by those whom they cannot otherwise have as faithful servants, they freely come, although they falsely say that they are compelled. It is therefore not to be wondered at, excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to submit to depraved and perverse men. to obey men whom, as we say, malice has made like themselves, and destructiveness toward the human race has made to be in agreement with them. But far be it from every Christian to wish to command demons through a depraved likeness of will; for if anyone begins in this life to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the future he will burn with them without end.

But why can good and just men not command the holy angels of God, into whose likeness of good will they have passed? I think that from what has already been said the solution of this question would easily be given, if the difference of understandings is recalled to mind. For although many men are established in the Church of God whose righteousness benefits many unto salvation, nevertheless very few in our times advance so far that, by the merit of holiness, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it happens that men of our age neither command malignant spirits by merit of holiness, nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of holiness by which, performing miracles in the Church, the saints once advanced, then they are already able powerfully both to command demons and to have familiar fellowship with the blessed spirits.

For it is certain that holy men beloved by God in the primitive Church of Christians once bestowed greater benefits upon mortals by the cooperation of good spirits than the impiety of depraved men could ever have inflicted harms by the ministry of demons. For whoever, as a true worshiper of God, has become like the holy angels can do many wondrous things by prayers.

On the Power of Witches.

Question Six

Question Sixth

The sixth question of your unconquered Majesty was: Whence comes this power so great in witches, by which they can accomplish so many various and wondrous things, even in one hour, such and so great things as none of the good could do in his whole life? To this question, if we wish to answer briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything.

For he says in the holy Gospel of Christ: Without me you can do nothing. Hence it is manifest that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God and from nowhere else, whether human beings do good or do evil. Hence the most holy Father Augustine says: The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing happens visibly in this whole, most ample and immense commonwealth of creation that is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments.

Therefore there is no doubt, Caesar, that that power of witches, by which, with the cooperation of demons, they produce wondrous and horrifying effects, is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a human being cannot even move his hand. For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a human being or a beast, unless almighty God wills it, consents to it, and grants the power, so that he may do what he has determined beforehand by his will. Unless God consents and wills, no creature has any power at all.

Otherwise, if anything could be done when he did not will and consent to it, it would necessarily follow that God was weak, since he could not prevent what he would be forced to permit against his will. But since every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both the will and the power.

Whatever witches do, therefore, is done by God permitting it; without his will they can do nothing. For unless God had granted that they could do what they wish, they would obtain it neither from themselves nor from demons. Thus all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved, as in the first cause of all things; for from him from whom we have received freedom of choice, from him also we have the power to do what we will.

But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they do not perpetrate the evils they do by human art, but by the cooperation of demons. Nature has made these demons subtle, and long experience has made them swift in producing wonders. For the wondrous effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and the like, but by the devil who instituted these signs; since he is most proud, he desires in all things to be seen as comparable to God.

Indeed, just as almighty God instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which, when worthily administered, signify and produce a saving effect with his own assistance, he who instituted them working salvation, so also the devil, who desires nothing more than to be thought equal to God, instituted certain signs as sacraments. When invoked by those with whom he has been joined by pacts, the malignant worker assists them, and as often as God permits, he brings about the evil that is requested; if God does not permit it, he does absolutely nothing.

For the devil is the worker of all the effects of necromancers and witches. By applying the means which he himself first instituted to the subject matter, he produces the desired work, sometimes in reality, sometimes only in appearance. But witch-women, who have now passed by depraved will and consent into the fellowship of demons through pacts, receive from them certain marks and symbolic signs, by which the demons, once summoned, immediately appear. In these destructive operations of demons nothing is stronger than the foolish credulity of witches, which is increased by pacts and vows; for the firmer the faith they have placed either in demons or in their signs, the more swiftly they obtain the operation, as the demons cooperate with them. For the too-savage depravity of the witches’ will turns them in a certain way into frenzy; and when this has seized their mind, the demons immediately attach themselves to them in their madness and, invited by pacts and signs, with God permitting it, furnish the effect of destruction to them in their insanity.

Plato recounts something similar in the book On Poetic Frenzy, saying: “Just as Bacchant women, when not of sound mind, draw honey and milk from rivers, but when of sound mind cannot draw them. Their spirit, carried outside itself into fellowship with an evil demon, brings this about.” We have ascertained that witches, at certain times, have drawn butter from stirred-up rivers; this cannot in any way be done otherwise than by the ministry of a demon.

In the same way, when they have been led into hatred of some person or animal, and sigh for its destruction, they are driven by a most grievous frenzy, thinking of nothing in their mind except vengeance. They take up things known and familiar to them for witchcraft, invoke demons, display the signs instituted by them, and at the same time the characters; and what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they accomplish by their agency

...they obtain by that ministry. But another person, who is not subject to the demons by pact and dedication, even if he knows the things suited to witchcraft and also the manner of working, and although he displays the signs, nevertheless rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the demons’ familiars. For the devil, swollen with pride, imitates the Church of Christ to such a degree that, just as an unordained man cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may utter the words of consecration, so also a demon either never or rarely comes to the aid of one who invokes him and shows his signs or characters, if he does not know that person to be subject to him by pact.

For if he came indiscriminately to all who invoked him without pacts having been made, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership. Hence many who are given over to profane arts, striving by dreadful conjurations to call demons to a circle, a mirror, or any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either God’s command stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious man who has not been dedicated to him by homage. For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is agreed that none is perpetrated:

fury in the mind and a depraved will in the witch, the cooperation also of a familiar demon, and before all else divine permission. If one of these does not concur, witchcraft cannot be perpetrated. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not meet the will of the wicked woman, she would perpetrate no witchcraft. Again, if the witch were lacking, the devil would by no means bring the witchcraft to completion.

For the devil uses the will of the raging witch as an artisan uses an instrument for working; without it he could not inflict witchcraft. And just as demons differ from one another in power and in sharpness of subtlety, so the power of a witch is not one and the same in all, but differs in each, according as demons of a subtler or grosser nature concur with them. For there are many kinds of demons, and they stand apart from one another by fixed degrees, according to the places into which they were cast down when they fell in the beginning.

The first kind of demons is called fiery; it ranges about the upper air and will never be plunged down to the lower regions before the day of judgment, but, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions,

has no commerce with human beings on earth. That they remain beneath the moon is attested by Saint Augustine in the work On the Christian Combat, saying thus: Demons do not dwell in the heaven where the sun and stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region.

Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, and for this reason Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals, fitted with little wings, have often been seen flying about; they spend their whole life in fire, since they arise with the fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to their own place from which they had come. They have no fellowship with witches, since, because of their subtlety, they dwell in fire and cannot assume a gross or airy body.

The second kind is called airy; wandering in the air, it dwells near us. Indeed they can descend to the lower regions and, by assuming bodies from the denser air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. By God’s permission they often disturb the air, stir up thunder and storms, and all conspire together for the destruction of the human race. They are moved by the passions of human affections, especially pride and envy, and are touched... and are touched by continual disturbances; they are neither clothed with a solid body nor do they remain in one place. Nor do they all have one form, but many, and they change these quite often according to the variety of their affections, either when they come, summoned by the spells of witches, or when, driven by disturbance, they are impelled to do harm. For they have an altogether violent and furious disposition, full of disturbances. Hence, being exceedingly wicked and disordered, they very often contrive sudden ambushes; and while they make their assaults, some wish to lie hidden, others inflict violence. Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are the more powerful for working witchcraft, the higher in their order the demon they have obtained as an accomplice.

In the life of Saint ANTONY, the divine Athanasius said that the air is full of demons; Hermes Trismegistus had also said this before, namely that no part of the world is bereft of the presence of demons. The holy bishop AMBROSE also says: “The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickednesses.” Hence the Platonists have handed down that demons flying in the air, like very dense fiery snow, become visible to those who desire it, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they keep their gaze fixed toward heaven with unblinking eyes. But I do not know whether the object in the air is caused by a real substance, or whether the checked motion of the eyes represents false images; nevertheless, though not without some injury to the sense, yet a slight one, I have made trial of the things just mentioned.

The third kind is called that of terrestrial demons, whom we do not in the least doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth for their own deserts. Concerning these, that most holy bishop and martyr of CHRIST, Theophorus, once Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: “Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and terrestrial spirits alike is made void.” Of these demons, some dwell in woods and groves, laying snares for hunters; others live in open fields, making travelers wander off course at night; some dwell in hidden places and caverns; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight in dwelling obscurely with human beings. They are not led by one affection, but by various ones, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Some of these rejoice in frightening human beings with mere illusions; others desire to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves by predictions of future events. Some, however, strive with the greatest effort to terrify, injure, or kill human beings troubled by irrational frenzy or raging with melancholy; and we have learned by experience that this has often happened. Hence Saint JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: “The greatness of grief is more powerful than every action of the devil in preventing harm; for whomever a demon overcomes, he overcomes through grief. If you take that away, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon.” This kind of demon, however, is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy of their affections and the lightness by which they delight more in terrifying many people than in being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet sometimes, to flatter the insane, they dwell in glass or in crystal or in a mirror, and, stirred up by spells, they give answers to women, and announce beforehand if someone coming to them has cursed them on the road. And this kind of witch sometimes differs greatly from the rest, because what those others make infirm by witchcraft, these promise to cure. But because they very often repel witchcraft by witchcraft, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, because, immersing itself in waters, it dwells around lakes and rivers, full of anger, troubled, restless, and deceitful. It raises storms at sea, sinks ships into the deep, and takes life from many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, it more often appears in the female sex, and is more rarely seen in the male, because they dwell in watery places and follow a softer manner of life, nor can they easily assume the vile form of the others by customary practice. Hence antiquity long ago named Naiads, Nereids, and nymphs of the waters not in the masculine sex but in the feminine. Among our people they are called, in the common vocabulary, aquatic women, that is, wasser frauwen. But those who dwell in drier and somewhat arid places, whenever they appear bodily to human beings ...appear bodily and visibly, they transform themselves into men. They also assume different forms of beasts, according as they are affected by various passions. But saints or angels, because they are not varied by passions, always appear uniformly in male form. For nowhere do we read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast, but always in a male form. Demons, however, have often been seen around rivers and springs in the form of women, sometimes dancing, sometimes spreading out their hair in the manner of women, and sometimes speaking with human beings and practicing various deceptions. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have dealings with witches.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. These demons are the worst in disposition, and they especially attack those who dig wells and mines, and those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make openings in the earth, stir up flame-breathing winds, and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes, coming out from the mountains by night in troops, they lead marvelous and astonishing dances in the fields; and, as though fearing the command of one leader, they suddenly vanish at a signal and return to their hiding places. At times the sound of bells is heard among them, and sometimes they falsely claim that they are the spirits of human beings who have departed this life. They seek nothing more than the fear and amazement of human beings. Hence we have found that they have sometimes led certain simpler people into their hiding places in the mountains, showing astonishing sights to those who marveled; and, as though the dwellings of the blessed were there, they falsely claim to be friends of the living.

Among these demons, too, some brood over the treasures that the greed of mortals has hidden in the earth; and lest they come again into human use, they carry them off, steal them, guard them, and sometimes transfer them from place to place. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have any dealings with women’s witchcraft.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they especially dread and detest the light: for they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any way except by night. This is the business that walks about in darkness: an inscrutable and utterly dark kind of demons, driven by cold passions,

The sixth kind of demons: light-fleeing. malicious, restless, and disturbed. It violently oppresses people whom it meets in the hours of night, and more often, when God permits, kills some either by its breath or by its touch. This kind of demon does not consort with witches, nor can it be constrained by incantations, because it flees both light and the voices of human beings, and likewise every disturbance of the air.

The aerial kind is especially accustomed to come to women’s witchcraft, because it is subtler than all the others and of the boldest rashness. Some of the terrestrial demons also, as has been said, serve acts of witchcraft; yet, being held to be of a lower rank, they cannot bring about those greater acts of witchcraft. It is therefore plainly established that the whole power of witches, by which they do such astonishing things, is granted to demons within limits set by the Lord God; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

On Divine Permission. Question Seven.

Question Seven

to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocents perish, grievously tortured?

I remember that, when I was long ago placed before your Majesty, I answered this question in this way: Almighty God, just and upright, kind and merciful, permits justly whatever he permits, because he is just, and there is no injustice with him; but all things that happen, he either does or permits in true judgment. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, we answer: he permits them because he is just.

Let the answer I have given not seem absurd to your Majesty, O Caesar, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For indeed, if he did not permit evils to be done, then man could not sin, and would certainly be impeccable; but that does not belong to his nature, to whom the Creator of all things gave free will from the beginning. For since man is a creature and not the Creator, he is necessarily capable of turning both to good and to evil, since his being depends on the supreme Maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends on the cause of its being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting. Every corruptible thing, however, necessarily falls away, yet is preserved by the goodness of the Creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor should have happened that man, by the condition of his nature, should be created impeccable, for this is enjoyed naturally only by God, the Maker of all things, who is unchangeable and everlasting.

But whenever it is granted to a man that he seems unable to sin, the freedom of the will is not taken away, nor is possibility simply removed, but the will is confirmed in the good. And whenever this gift is granted to a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel.

For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should both have free will and be unable to commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last, in glory, will be much more to be unable to sin. And so, if man could not sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, he nevertheless justly permits men to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of will remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its reward, and voluntary wickedness may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly.

Therefore almighty God justly permits men to sin and to do evil, to whom he granted freedom of will from the beginning. Now many reasons have long since been assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great acts of sorcery to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall necessarily make brief mention in order.

The first is that the excellence of the divine power may be manifested, for he alone is unchangeable and far above every position. Every mutable creature has no comparison with the unchangeable Creator. Hence it is read in Numbers: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit too it is written: You are just, O Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.

For he will repay a man according to his work, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness openly recognizes that he is nothing in comparison with his Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, both so that freedom of will may be preserved and so that the excellence of the great God may become known to men.

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, by which he knows how to draw good out of our evils, when he makes the sin of one person become a merit for another, for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, who would understand our good? For God makes and ordains the good; but evils he does not make, but, once they have been done by the impious, he himself disposes them so that they do not come about in disorder. Neither does the wickedness of men hinder the will of God, nor can man do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause, moreover, why the Almighty permits acts of sorcery to be done is that he may manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, neither could God be merciful. But since we all offend in many things, everywhere God finds something to forgive; everywhere a guilty person presents himself.

...the guilty person presents himself, in whom the gracious Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy prelate Augustine says: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised, not sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not be ended. Therefore where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, heaps together into one. Thus the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance; for if everyone acted well and no one sinned, God’s justice would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have its place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will repay each person according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse off than brute animals, which, with no violence compelling them, freely use the motions of nature. For although brute animals lack reason, nevertheless they freely possess the motion of nature which they follow; in comparison with them man would seem to be of an inferior condition if he did not freely have the choice of his will. But God permitted man a free will, which neither kings nor princes command. The sixth reason is the praise due to the merit of steadfast human virtue, when we praise a just man because, although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with God’s grace assisting him, remained steadfast in a good will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such great evil deeds through the intervention of witches is that those who, having despised the truth, delight in falsehood may be seduced and utterly deceived by the devil, the inventor of falsehood. For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who scorn to follow the saving teachings of Christ, should be deceived by demons and all plunged down to hell to be punished forever. They seek help from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have worshiped. For it is just that one who, of his own will, abandons the truth and adheres to falsehood should be hurled by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose might and virtue are above every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits the devil great things and denies him certain small things, he shows how weak the enemy of the human race is, and that he is subject in all things to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing by himself, but everything he does, he does with God permitting it.

Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits evil deeds to be done, is justice: by it he preserves, in inviolable order, the freedom that he granted to the creature once at the beginning. But because the power of every creature, dependent on its Creator, is restricted and limited, it is manifest that neither the devil can do everything he wishes, nor can a human being, however depraved in will. The will is indeed free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wished, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would make all things totter. Job 18.

The story of holy Job plainly demonstrates by example the bound power of demons: Satan did not dare to tempt him more than had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if they were always able to use freely, according to their own judgment, the power to harm.

Before the Lord’s passion they enjoyed greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power was thereafter greatly diminished, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” For the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the boldness of demons, so that they can rightly be called instigators of evils, but by no means compellers. Nor would the devil prevail against us unless he received strength from our sins. Hence Scripture warns us, saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” And again: “Do not give place to the devil.”

Therefore, in concluding this discourse for the understanding of the proposed question, why God permits so many acts of maleficium to occur, I believe I have made the reasons sufficiently clear. For even if the will of demons is always wicked, their power can never be unjust, since what they wickedly will they have from their own choice, but what they are able wickedly to do they have from God alone. And these things have been said insofar as they concern those who do evil. But why does almighty God permit demons to harm, through the agency of witches, people who have been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the wicked, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and possessions, but were kept away from approach to and injury of the good and faithful, the judgment of this permission would rightly seem to be just. But now more often the good and innocent are weakened by the demons’ acts of maleficium and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods which those bewitched often suffer. It troubles many people why the Almighty permits these things, he who permits nothing unjustly.

For this question now proposed, I shall briefly set out in order, as far as I can, the necessary reasons, no others than those I have received from the ancient and Catholic teachers. The first reason, then, is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity, so that, when scourged by the demons’ maleficia, they may learn in the sufferings of the flesh what faith and love for God they possess in the hidden part of the mind. In prosperity it is not difficult to be long-suffering, but in adversity to await the Savior’s help with humble patience is not the mark of the soft, but of the strong and of truly faithful Christians. In his own tribulation most holy Job learned how great a confidence of faith he had in God, he who previously, in tranquillity, had preserved piety without the dart of temptation.

At the same time it should be noted from this that those whom the maleficia of demons or human beings have in any way made ill, and who, in order to recover health, either approach or consult malefici and enchanters, or do this either through themselves or through others against the precepts of God and the Church, have neither true faith in God nor love. For they put the health of mortal flesh before God, and seek salvation not from Christ, but from the devil and his minister. They prefer to live healthy, but unhappily, in the name of the devil, rather than to suffer a little here for love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever.

But someone who does not approach malefici because God has forbidden it, preferring to live in poverty and sickness while observing God’s commandments rather than against God in wealth and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith. Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, people corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith are not to be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by maleficia, who reveal thefts and adulteries through the ministry of demons, and who foretell future things by inspecting stones or mirrors. I beg you, do not listen to those who, ignorant of the divine laws, [unclear] ministers The second reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by sorcery is the increase of merits: namely, so that, when their patience has been tested in tribulation, it may more worthily deserve the crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a person is unknown to himself as to what he can bear and what he cannot. Sometimes he fears that he cannot bear what he nevertheless can; when temptation arrives, as if some examiner were questioning him, he is discovered by himself, who before, hidden, did not know himself.

The blessed chief apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others as being thoughtless and weak; that temptation came, and the weakness that lay hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest testing of a person, as sacred Scripture attests: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just people.” Patience is easy in prosperity, when no adversities strike the mind. “But the tribulations of the just are many; from all these our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.”

The third reason for divine permission is the preservation of humility, so that a faithful and just person may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or justice. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men. Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with iniquity; from their impiety, as if from fat, their iniquity has come forth.” It belongs to the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and just people to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable fortune would have made proud.

Finally, the fearful imagining of sorceries makes a good person fear his God and diligently call upon his help, so that, fortified by it against the assaults of demons, he may be able to trust that he is safe. But let no one who is proud and presumptuous of his own strength think himself safe from the sorceries of demons, because the person whom, swollen with pride, God’s protection abandons undoubtedly lies open to the sorceries of demons.

The fourth reason is so that there may be a distinction between the good and the evil. For Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning good people beloved by God: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

And Saint Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.” The most wise King Solomon also says in Proverbs: “Whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and as a father he is pleased with his son.” It is a Christian thing, and not without glory, to endure adversities patiently for God’s love, whether they are brought on by evil people or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and just people not for their ruin, as the perverse suppose, but rather for the very great and certain consolation of the soul.

Indeed, when a just person lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does wrong to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeping his commandments with all care, and is nevertheless afflicted by sorceries, whether in body, in possessions, or in both, that person is truly blessed; for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the Catholic Church of Christians, and who, receiving evils in this world, patiently endures them for God’s love, has a sure sign that he will persevere in God’s grace and be saved. On the contrary...

On the contrary, concerning the wicked and the reprobate we read it written thus: “Why do the impious live, raised up and strengthened with riches? Their houses are secure and at peace, and the rod of God is not upon them. They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they go down to hell.” For it is a manifest sign of damnation if you live wickedly here in sins and vices, opposed to God, and yet prosper in the goods of fortune and in bodily health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and righteous people to be troubled by the wicked and reprobate is for the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.” But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, by mercy he ordains temporal punishments for righteous people for their offenses, but by justice eternal punishments for the impious and reprobate. Therefore by mercy he changes eternal punishment for the penitent into temporal punishment, which they must suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very grave, the merciful God, loving the penitent, has been accustomed to purify them in this life in various ways, through diverse hardships of tribulations in body and in possessions. For the sorceries of the impious benefit good and righteous people as a remedy, but bring damnation upon those who inflict them.

The sixth reason is so that a man bewitched through assaults of demons may be recalled to repentance and may resolve in his heart upon the necessary amendment of life. For Almighty God does not immediately send vengeance when we sin, but waits for our amendment until the appointed time. But if we neglect to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect him; and we who, while sinners, scorned to acknowledge ourselves by repenting in tranquility will at last, though late, acknowledge ourselves in tribulation. Hence the holy prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: “If his sons forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes; but my mercy I will not scatter from them, nor will I harm them in my truth.”

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the sorceries of demons to prevail against the good and innocent is so that he may cut away from them an excessively unrestrained occasion for sinning. For there are many poor and sick people, pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom poverty and bodily illness preserve in the love of God; if they were rich and raised up with honors, they would quickly flow down from the purpose of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a man better. Therefore Almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, the righteous, and the innocent to be subject to various calamities. And sometimes through demons, sometimes through wicked people, and sometimes in diverse other ways and by other means, he turns riches and honors away from people of this sort, knowing beforehand that they would make bad use of them, so that they may keep humility in poverty and abasement, which they certainly would not have preserved if placed in opulence and high rank. He also quite often permits them to fall into many and great illnesses, when joyous bodily health would have brought very great sickness upon the mind. Finally, he permits certain people to be driven to death by sorcery, so that the license for sinning may be cut away from them, a license they would have abused if allowed to remain longer in life. Hence Scripture says of the righteous man: “He was taken away lest malice change his understanding, and lest deceit beguile his soul.”

The eighth reason for divine permission is so that people may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which possess great They have great power against all sorceries of malignant spirits. For one who venerates the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church with due honor is rarely harmed by the sorceries of demons. And from the witches’ own confession we have quite often heard that attendance at Masses and the use of things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. Nor do they bless these things in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be feared tokens, showing demons the defenses of divine protection. Concerning boys and infants, however, who, having been reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the sorceries of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by sorceries because of the sins of their parents.

On the Providence of God.

Question Eight

This was the eighth question of your Serenity: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as it can by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and has a certain and infallible providence over all and each of the things that are done in the world.

I remember replying to this question as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence; by its will and command they were brought into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us briefly establish this opinion, first from the Scriptures and then by arguments, as far as is permitted.

In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise king Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth so as to make your soul sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered by your words, destroy all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies of providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and not one of them falls upon the earth before God?” This is a great commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for human beings, but also for the smallest birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for greater things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little afterward he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, O you of little faith?”

Almighty God, because he created all things and brought them into being when they did not exist, rules and governs the whole universe lest they slip and fall away. This could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, the ordered continuity of the whole universe must necessarily be thrown into confusion. The Creator’s providence cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives beasts their food, fills every living creature with blessing, and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful splendor, cannot forget the human being whom he created from the beginning in his own image. He who governs all things cares for all things, and he has providence not only over human beings, but also over all beasts; all things are placed under his rule, and there is nothing that can resist his will in anything. Therefore let us now consider this immense structure of the whole universe: how, in its original disposition and motion, it has always continued most orderly, and divine

that unchangeable divine providence preserves, directs, and governs them, unless we disgracefully lose our senses, we shall understand by the clearest reasoning. Then let us contemplate all earthly things, how each and every one of them is born and proceeds in its own natural disposition in the most orderly way. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created. Next, let us consider the earth, placed in the middle of the world like a point or center, which unfolds the circle of the whole universe at an equal distance. Nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing, finally, more delightful could present itself to the sense for contemplation. In this point of an immense mass, wonderfully enclosed by that very mass, we see all things ordered, and we see that nothing can be left unordered, so that whatever sometimes seems to us somehow to drift, we may know with certainty that, within the order of the universe, it does not lack its own particular order. For by God’s simple and wholly unchangeable nod, the whole structure of the entire universe, assembled from so many diverse and movable things, works together in the most orderly way and is governed. We certainly see in those things that present themselves to our senses that, the greater the intelligence and power that arises over time in any governor, the less can anything disordered occur there by random chance.

Therefore, since that supreme intellect, the creator, preserver, and ruler of all things, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, no place is ever left for rash chance, which might obstruct the will of so great a majesty. Thus the whole universe, whatever exists anywhere or can exist, is contained under the command of the one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. Unexpected events happen to us because we are changeable and are changed almost every day, having no determinate knowledge of future things. But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, and understands all things at once and together. His providence is not deceived; his will is never varied; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never interrupted, even if at times his judgment seems to be changed. Hence, if we attend carefully, we shall plainly understand, as the ends and order of motions will declare, that all these lower things are made, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence, from whose command absolutely nothing is alien.

For God himself, the creator of the universe, both understands all things and is not divided in a particular way, as we are, into many things, but remains in himself an indivisible one. By beholding himself as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes, he contemplates the cause of all things through their causes; and by contemplating all things he cares for them and provides for them, directing each thing to a good end by an everlasting order. Come now, most wise Celsus: in order that we may understand divine providence governing all things, let us use arguments, as far as we can, more briefly for our purpose.

Thus, if God’s action is his own proper understanding, which no wise person will deny, as the most eminent and at the same time the most inward thing, then as much as he acts, so much in any case he understands, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but also in the very smallest. Therefore he understands individual things. For the first being, through individual things that are in any way beings, following upon fixed orders, is the most ample cause; and the things that act after him are everywhere moved by his power and act by it. Either, then, God understands or acts nothing outside himself, which is false, or, by acting all things and each thing, he also understands those same things, which is true. For they would never come into being unless they were first, to speak in our manner, understood by God himself, who makes them, just as things are not brought into being by the sun and not first seen by it. But because all things And all individual things that the Almighty makes, he understands.

There is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made, from whom things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from him too they have received the proper office of a cause, that is, to preserve as far as their powers allow and to care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, with good reason that first cause has this natural goodness and providence, so that it cares for all things and every individual thing that it has made, inasmuch as it is most truly the cause of all of them and of each one.

Indeed, unless the things that preserve common realities in individuals are guarded individually by him who makes them, those common realities are never guarded. For one will not preserve the whole, which consists of parts, if the parts themselves are neglected. Therefore, from the intention of the first, greatest, and most common intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things; but that intelligence itself distinguishes all other things from others in themselves, and distinguishes the rest among themselves by the rule of its own conception. Hence, just as God knows all things and each individual thing most distinctly, so too he most distinctly rules, moderates, and cares for them.

I think it is therefore manifest, most merciful Emperor Maximilian, and sufficiently shown, that the providence of God, the highest ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and moderates all lower things and each individual thing; for otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who watches over them, they could in no way maintain this most beautiful order that we discern. Nor does it escape me how variously the wise men of this world once held opinions concerning providence. Some of them thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance. If their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift, since the world could perish by the same chance by which it was made.

Against their false opinion, others taught that the world could neither have been made without reason nor certainly continue to exist unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, creator of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity, and, remaining steadfast, give all things motion.” And again he said: “The generation of all things, the whole progression of changeable natures, and whatever is moved, in some way draws its causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.”

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly bodies and separate substances, together with the species, and that he truly did not know all the rest at all and utterly neglected them. But these men erred shamefully, because the Almighty has providence and care not only for all incorruptible things, but also for particular and corruptible things. Hence Saint Boethius again says: “The high creator sits upon the summit, and, ruling all things, turns the reins: king and lord, fountain and origin, law and wise judge of equity. This is the common bond of things, the continuous love by which they seek to be held by the end of the good; for otherwise they cannot endure unless, with love turned back again, the causes flow back to him who gave them.”

Some, not tolerating the thought that they themselves should be neglected, removed man from the number of corruptible things because of the excellence of his intellect, saying that God has care and providence for man, but despises all the remaining earthly things. Against their false opinion, I think enough has already been said, and to produce many more arguments would be altogether superfluous. For Scripture says: “You will save men and beasts, Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has care alike for all.”

Therefore divine majesty’s providence orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all lower things and each individual thing, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; its most powerful will made all things from nothing.

He produced all things, as sacred Scripture again bears witness: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.” Therefore let those men blush who are corrupt in mind, impious, and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, who, puffed up with vain talkativeness, take away the providence of him who knows all things and do not consider how great an injury they do to God.

For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he foresees nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has already lost all dignity. Yet, as Saint Anselm attests, it is impossible for God to lose his honor; for, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, no corruption, and no sin. Therefore whoever removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what is he saying except that God does not exist?

But let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things now tell me this. If God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is no longer any reason why we should pursue him with worship or venerate him with religion, since from him we obtain no benefit; rather, being neglected and despised, let us neglect him ourselves. But if, not knowing us, he despises and neglects us, then there is plainly no reason why we should worship one who does not know us and, for that reason, cannot bestow any good, or invoke him with prayers.

For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every reason for piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is taken away, whom do we worship? whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, surely he neither bestows benefits on human beings, nor imposes punishments on deserters; he neither can help mortals, nor wishes to, nor cares at all, nor notices what we do, and he hears neither the prayers nor the petitions of anyone.

Why, then, do we offer him any worship? Why honor, and why prayers? Or why do we so greatly dread or fear a God who does not know us, who, once we have been neglected and despised by him, can do us neither good nor harm? For once providence has been removed, neither holiness nor religion will endure; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and a dreadful confusion will follow. Once piety toward God has been removed, what will the commonwealth be but everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings, the fellowship of the human race, and justice will necessarily perish; all these will vanish and perish together.

What must be thought of the Christian faith, if God does not care for human affairs? What, then, of the savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ? Unless there is a providence of God caring for mortal things, one will regard him as nothing but an empty tale and a wholly fictitious thing. Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is all vain and useless to us if he has no care for us at all.

Let those who deny the providence of God now see and be horrified, when they behold the sane outcome of their own opinion: the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, clothed in the vain speech of secular philosophers, train himself to contempt of God; let no one remove the providence of the highest and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of, and ungrateful for, the benefits of the most merciful savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole universe, both visible and invisible, and all things individually, whether they are in heaven or on earth or in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is alien to his care. For crops, too, and all the other things that the earth brings forth, as well as storms and the variations of the weather and of the sky, [unclear]. and the changes by which all things that the earth brings forth, once brought into being, grow to maturity: divine providence provides and procures all and each of these for the human race, not only the great things but also the smallest, so far that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it, rules it, and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this whole vast magnitude of the universe cannot be ruled and governed by one God, who alone exists, he is greatly mistaken, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. For indeed, he who could bring the whole world from nothing into being can also govern forever, most wisely, what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, and can do all things, who alone, almighty, created all things. Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence; and let us raise our minds upward from these passing things with what strength we can, and, brought back into ourselves, be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God present everywhere. Since it is wholly uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. Yet it does not sustain from one side and surpass from another, nor fill from one side and encompass from another; rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. Through bodily bulk he is nowhere, and through his uncircumscribable substance he is nowhere absent; he is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart. O inexplicable power, O incomprehensible goodness, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity: you do not consist of parts like a body, nor are you set apart by passions like a soul, nor do you underlie forms like all the other things that were made by you. You are in all things and above all things, ruling and governing the universe most wisely.

By these testimonies, then, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, it has, as I think, been sufficiently proved that this whole universe is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and eternal, he knows all things, understands all things, recognizes all things; and since by nature he is almighty, he can do all things, to whom nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. He created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by strength, and illumines them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, glorious and exalted God, forever and ever. Amen.

The author's declaration to Caesar.

These, unconquered Caesar Maximilian, are the things that it seemed to me should be said in response to the eight questions proposed by your Majesty. For you wished to have from me a judgment on them in writing also, judging me, beyond the truth, more highly than is fitting; for I am not to be compared in ability with those whose opinions you heard before me. Let this make me worthy of pardon if I have said something less fitting: that, being on the road by command of Your Highness, I dictated, as I could, in haste, what occurred to me as needing response.

But I say from my heart and openly declare that I am a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, and that I wish to remain until death in union with the most holy Roman Church. Therefore, if in this little work of mine or in others I should have said or written anything otherwise than she holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, as a son of true obedience, by the attestation of the present writing I deny it, and I wish it simply and forever to be held as revoked. Therefore, wisest Caesar, I both humbly ask and earnestly warn your Majesty that, before you bring my responses to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined, you have them rejected by the judgment of many. For it must be taken care of with the greatest effort that nothing be set before those for whose salvation Your Serenity keeps watch, unless it is sound, approved, clear, and lawfully confirmed in the Catholic faith by the judgment of very many wise men. May almighty God by his providence direct and guard you always, to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors.
